strengths: Soundness: The central formulation is principled. Decomposing attention over concatenated blocks into locally normalized outputs and unnormalized mass correctly motivates matching both quantities; the per-token bias addresses the otherwise unavoidable mass deficit when t<T.

Originality: Directly fitting compact keys, biases, and values through OMP/NNLS/least squares is a novel and useful alternative to end-to-end latent-cache optimization. The treatment of logical versus physical cache length and reusable nonuniform head budgets is also insightful.

Significance: Across three model families and two substantially different long-context QA benchmarks, the proposed methods generally establish a strong quality–compaction-time trade-off, especially at 20–100x compaction. The reported reduction from hours for Cartridges to seconds or minutes could be practically important.

The evaluation contains meaningful ablations of biases, fitted values, nonuniform budgets, on-policy queries, and self-study. It also reports component-level timing on a 60k-token context and includes a promising repeated-compaction AIME experiment.

Presentation and reproducibility are mostly strong: the paper is clearly organized, supplies derivations, pseudocode, model and dataset details, baseline configurations, prompt templates, numerical-stability choices, and solver implementation details. No material ethical issue is apparent from the experiments themselves.
weaknesses: Soundness: The concatenation argument is exact only when output and mass matching hold for future queries, whereas the method fits a finite, context-specific proxy query set. There is no error propagation or generalization analysis explaining when this proxy remains valid after multiple layers, future decoding, or distribution shift; the empirical evidence partially supports but does not resolve this central gap.

The empirical uncertainty is underreported. QuALITY uses 50 contexts, LongHealth only four aggregated contexts, and most plots provide neither confidence intervals nor repeated-run variability. Evaluation uses each model's default, potentially stochastic decoding settings, so small differences between methods cannot be judged reliably.

The strongest component—nonuniform budgeting—appears to be calibrated using QuALITY contexts, but the manuscript does not clearly identify a disjoint calibration split or include the one-time sensitivity-estimation cost. This creates possible evaluation-set tuning and makes the headline timing comparison incomplete.

Several comparisons are limited or potentially unfavorable to the baselines: Cartridges is evaluated only for Qwen on 20 QuALITY contexts using a default, explicitly unoptimized recipe, while question-aware SnapKV and PyramidKV are converted to a different question-agnostic setting using one synthetic mock question. These are defensible adaptations, but they do not support an unrestricted claim of outperforming the original methods.

Practical deployment evidence is incomplete. Learned per-head biases and nonuniform per-head lengths require specialized attention-mask and variable-length cache integration, yet the paper benchmarks offline compaction rather than end-to-end memory, decoding throughput, or latency in an inference engine. The claim of negligible-to-zero attention-runtime overhead is therefore not directly demonstrated.

Reproducibility has concrete defects despite the detailed appendix: Algorithm 2 loops t times while selecting k keys per iteration, apparently returning kt keys rather than the stated budget; Algorithm 3's iteration indexing is also inconsistent. No code/artifact, seeds, exact decoding parameters, or full numeric result tables are provided, and some dense figure labels are effectively unreadable.

The limitations discussion honestly covers runtime and degradation at extreme ratios, but should also discuss calibration leakage, statistical uncertainty, required kernel support, privacy/security implications of latent caches retaining sensitive context, and the narrow evaluation scope. Overall, this is a technically promising and useful contribution, but these issues keep the evidence and deployability short of a clear Accept.

strengths: Soundness/originality: The attention-matching formulation is well motivated. Matching both locally normalized attention outputs and unnormalized attention mass correctly preserves a block’s contribution when arbitrary KV blocks are concatenated, and the per-token bias addresses the otherwise unavoidable mass deficit when t<T. Combining this with NNLS/least-squares fitting and subset-based key selection is a novel and technically coherent contribution.

Significance: Fast, post-hoc KV compaction without model training addresses an important deployment bottleneck. Results across three model families, QuALITY, and LongHealth suggest a useful speed-quality frontier, including strong performance at 20–50× compaction and substantial speedups over Cartridges.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear and unusually explicit about logical versus physical cache length, positional handling, chunking, query construction, solver choices, and baseline adaptations. Ablations support the value of fitted biases, values, and nonuniform head budgets.

Limitations/ethics: The authors candidly acknowledge that OMP variants remain slow, Cartridges can win at more extreme compression, compact keys are restricted to original keys, and systems integration remains unfinished. The work has no obvious severe ethical risk.
weaknesses: Soundness: The strongest downstream claims lack uncertainty estimates or statistical testing. QuALITY has only 50 independently compacted contexts, LongHealth has only four, and many questions share each compacted cache; treating hundreds of questions as independent would overstate evidence. Generation uses stochastic model defaults, yet seeds and repeated-run variability are not reported. Only the sensitivity illustration includes error bars.

Evaluation leakage is insufficiently ruled out. The crucial nonuniform budgets are derived from sensitivity curves averaged over QuALITY contexts, apparently including the same first validation articles used for evaluation. The manuscript does not identify a disjoint calibration split. Because removing the learned head budget is the largest ablation degradation, held-out calibration and cross-dataset transfer experiments are needed.

Baseline coverage and comparability are limited. Cartridges is evaluated only for Qwen on a 20-context subset, while several pruning baselines are modified from their original question-aware or online settings using a synthetic mock question. These are reasonable adaptations, but they do not establish broad dominance over the original methods. Exact numerical results and paired comparisons are also unavailable because the principal results appear only as dense plots.

The systems evidence is incomplete relative to the deployment framing. Timings are reported for isolated compaction components on single high-end GPUs, but there is no end-to-end decoding throughput, peak-memory, batching, or kernel benchmark with learned biases and variable per-head lengths. The claimed negligible runtime overhead and practical benefit of nonuniform packing are therefore not demonstrated. Gemma ratios also cover only global-attention layers, limiting direct comparison with full-cache ratios.

Reproducibility is only moderate: no code or artifact is identified; random seeds, exact model decoding settings, software versions, the calibration contexts/grid/cost for sensitivity curves, and several head-budget hyperparameters are missing. Algorithm 2 also loops t times while selecting k keys per iteration, which would select kt keys rather than the stated budget unless the loop bound is corrected.

Presentation and scope: Figure 3 is crowded and does not provide exact values, while the online-compaction result is a small proof of concept on one model and 30 AIME problems. Claims that it can decouple reasoning depth from physical limits or support arbitrary long-horizon generation are premature. The limitations section should also discuss evaluation leakage, statistical uncertainty, custom-kernel requirements, and possible privacy or clinical-use concerns around medical-record workloads.

strengths: Originality/significance: Attention Matching is a compelling formulation of latent KV-cache compaction. Matching both locally normalized attention outputs and unnormalized attention mass is well motivated by the block-mixture identity and directly addresses compatibility with subsequently appended tokens.

Soundness: The decomposition into key selection, nonnegative bias fitting, and least-squares value fitting is technically intuitive and largely well specified. The per-token biases have a clear role: without them, retaining a key subset necessarily underestimates the original block's attention mass.

Evaluation: Results span three model families, full-attention and sliding-window architectures, two substantially different long-context QA benchmarks, and compaction ratios reaching 50–100×. Attention Matching generally establishes a strong quality–compaction frontier and the component ablations support the proposed biases, fitted values, reference-query construction, and nonuniform budgets.

Practical significance: The approach avoids per-context end-to-end training and reduces compaction from several GPU-hours for Cartridges to seconds or minutes. The faster highest-attention variant and higher-quality OMP variant provide a useful deployment trade-off.

Presentation/reproducibility: The paper is clearly written and provides equations, pseudocode, prompts, solver details, baseline configurations, timing breakdowns, and a candid limitations discussion. The preliminary repeated-compaction experiment also identifies a promising extension without overstating it as a finished result.
Ethics: The work presents no evident major ethical concern, and its potential to lower inference-memory and compute requirements is beneficial.
weaknesses: Soundness: Preservation under arbitrary appended tokens is exact only when mass and attention outputs match for the realized query. The method fits these quantities on a finite proxy query distribution, while compaction itself can change later-layer queries. On-policy fitting mitigates this issue empirically but does not justify the strongest future-token language in general.

Evaluation: The headline downstream comparisons lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-run analysis. LongHealth contains only four aggregated contexts, so its 400 questions are strongly clustered rather than 400 independent samples; this makes several apparent accuracy differences difficult to interpret.

The Cartridges comparison is limited to Qwen3-4B and only 20 QuALITY articles, whereas most proposed-method results use 50 articles. The paper notes the subset's different full-cache accuracy but does not provide paired confidence intervals, weakening claims of definitively exceeding Cartridges.

The learned nonuniform head schedule is the most important ablated component, yet the paper does not clearly state that the ten QuALITY calibration articles used to derive sensitivity curves are disjoint from evaluation articles. A held-out calibration protocol and cross-dataset schedule-transfer results are needed to establish that this is genuinely reusable rather than transductive tuning.

Reproducibility: No code or ready-to-use learned head schedules are provided. Some implementation details are also inconsistent: Algorithm 2 loops for t iterations while selecting k keys per iteration, apparently returning kt keys rather than respecting budget t, and the routine called NNLS for OMP is actually an unconstrained least-squares solution followed by clamping when iterations are set to zero.

Systems evidence is incomplete. The paper measures compaction time, but it does not report end-to-end decoding latency, peak memory during compaction, or an integrated variable-length per-head attention implementation. Thus claims about negligible bias overhead and full compute benefits of nonuniform caches remain plausible but not demonstrated.

Scope is still limited to two QA datasets and models up to 12B parameters. The paper argues that KV dimensions scale mildly to larger MoE models, but this does not establish that query generation, model execution, numerical behavior, or downstream quality will scale similarly.

Ethics/limitations: The limitations discussion is useful, but the paper does not discuss privacy or governance considerations for compacting sensitive records such as the medical-style LongHealth contexts, nor possible information-recovery risks from latent caches. These are minor for the present benchmark study but relevant to the deployment motivation.

strengths: Soundness: The central formulation is well motivated. Decomposing attention over concatenated blocks into locally normalized outputs and unnormalized mass directly explains why both quantities must be preserved, and the scalar bias addresses the otherwise unavoidable mass mismatch when t<T.

Originality and significance: Refitting per-head biases and values through nonnegative and ordinary least squares, combined with subset-based key selection, is a useful and fairly novel alternative to both token eviction and expensive end-to-end latent-cache optimization. The resulting speed-quality trade-off could be practically important for long-context serving.

Evaluation breadth is unusually strong: results cover three model families and QuALITY, LongHealth, QASPER, LongBench v2, and RULER, including multiple-choice, generative, heterogeneous, and retrieval-heavy settings. Attention Matching generally improves substantially over strong token-selection and token-merging baselines, especially at 20x-100x compaction.

The paper provides informative ablations of biases, value fitting, nonuniform budgets, on-policy queries, and self-study. It also reports component-level runtime, examines reconstruction loss, tests a sliding-window architecture, and includes a promising repeated-compaction experiment on AIME.

Presentation is clear and technically detailed. The appendices provide algorithms, prompts, baseline adaptations, numerical-stability measures, chunking details, and solver descriptions. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges minute-scale costs, poorer behavior than Cartridges in some extreme-compaction cases, architectural incompatibility with MLA, and the preliminary status of online deployment.
No unresolved material ethical concern is apparent. The method may reduce inference memory, although the paper could discuss compute and clinical-data considerations more explicitly.
weaknesses: The main comparative evidence lacks uncertainty estimates or repeated-run statistics despite stochastic default decoding. Most accuracy curves report only point estimates, LongHealth contains just four aggregated contexts, and the claimed superiority over Cartridges is not statistically established.

The Cartridges comparison is not fully controlled: it is evaluated only on a 20-context QuALITY subset whose full-cache accuracy is 75.0%, while most other results use 50 contexts with 71.1% accuracy. Figure 1 nevertheless describes n=894 overall, making its direct Pareto comparison ambiguous. Cartridges is also run only for Qwen and with one default training configuration.

The nonuniform head-budget procedure is insufficiently separated from evaluation. Sensitivity curves are measured on QuALITY articles, but the manuscript does not clearly state whether calibration articles are disjoint from reported QuALITY test contexts. Since this component is the largest ablation gain, possible calibration-set leakage is important. Exact calibration data, discretization, step size, and schedules should be released.

Reproducibility is incomplete. No code or artifact availability statement is provided, and several consequential details are underspecified, including random seeds, exact decoding parameters rather than model defaults, NNLS iteration and power-iteration settings, sensitivity-curve grids, and complete timing methodology. The paper also repeatedly describes subproblems as closed-form even though NNLS and OMP are iterative and the implemented NNLS is an approximate projected-gradient procedure.

The practical systems claims outrun the evidence. Timings measure compaction components on single H100/H200 GPUs, but there is no integrated serving implementation or measurement of end-to-end latency, throughput, kernel overhead from learned attention biases, or variable-length per-head packing. Claims that biases have negligible-to-zero runtime cost and that asynchronous compaction adds no user-facing latency therefore remain plausible proposals rather than demonstrated results.

Generalization to arbitrary future queries is only guaranteed if matching is accurate on those queries; empirically the method relies on self-study and repeated-prefill queries as proxies. The paper should quantify held-out attention-output and mass errors, analyze distribution shift more directly, and connect these errors to downstream degradation.

The LongBench v2 subset is selected using full-context/no-context outcomes and contains only 47 examples. Although selection uses a separate stochastic run and all methods are re-evaluated, this conditional benchmark can inflate apparent preservation and has considerable sampling uncertainty; full-benchmark results or confidence intervals are needed.

Overall, this is a strong and likely useful contribution, but the uncontrolled comparisons, unclear calibration split, missing statistical treatment, and lack of an integrated serving evaluation keep it at weak accept rather than a confident accept.

strengths: Soundness: The core decomposition is well motivated: matching both locally normalized attention outputs and unnormalized attention mass is sufficient to preserve a block’s contribution under concatenation when those quantities are matched for the relevant queries. The learned per-key bias directly addresses the systematic mass loss caused by retaining fewer keys.

Originality: Combining mass-correcting biases, least-squares value fitting, reference-query sampling, and subset key selection provides a novel and practically useful alternative to end-to-end latent-cache optimization. The formulation produces several meaningful speed-quality operating points.

Significance: Results are broad and often substantial, covering three model families and QuALITY, LongHealth, QASPER, LongBench v2, RULER, and a preliminary online-compaction experiment. The gains over token-selection and token-merging baselines are especially compelling at 20x-100x compaction; the 6,500-example RULER evaluation is useful supporting evidence.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. It explains the attention-matching objective, implementation choices, ablations, computational breakdown, and limitations in considerable detail. The rendered figures and tables are legible.

The ablations support the importance of biases, fitted values, and nonuniform head allocation, while the reference-query experiments clarify the tradeoff between inexpensive repeat-prefill queries and self-study. The paper also honestly acknowledges slower OMP variants, degradation at extreme compression, incompatibility with MLA, and incomplete systems integration.

No major research-ethics problem is apparent. Critical prompt tokens can be excluded from compaction, and the reported failure behavior is mostly loss of specific information rather than incoherent output.
weaknesses: The paper does not validate its central systems assumptions end to end. It reports cache-compaction time but not decoding latency, throughput, peak memory, or implementation overhead in a serving engine. Per-key biases and per-head variable-length caches may require specialized kernels or layouts; the claim of negligible-to-zero attention-runtime cost is therefore insufficiently supported.

Several headline comparisons are not strictly like for like. Cartridges is evaluated only on Qwen and on 20 QuALITY contexts whose full-cache accuracy is 75.0%, whereas the main Attention Matching results use 50 contexts with 71.1% full-cache accuracy. Figure 1 nevertheless describes n=894 questions while including Cartridges results based on only 357, making the claim of exceeding Cartridges less conclusive than the figure suggests. Other baselines are modified from online or question-aware settings into a question-agnostic one-shot protocol, so the conclusions should be scoped to this deployment setting.

Statistical uncertainty is largely absent. LongHealth contains only four aggregated contexts, LongBench v2 uses a selected subset of 47 examples, and most accuracy plots provide no confidence intervals or repeated-run variation despite default stochastic decoding. Questions sharing a document are also correlated, so treating question counts as effective sample sizes would overstate certainty.

The LongBench v2 subset is selected using the same model’s full-context success and no-context failure. Although the selection run is separate, this produces a diagnostic conditional subset rather than evidence of benchmark-wide performance; its small size and nonmonotonic results further limit the generalization claim.

The theoretical guarantee applies only when mass and outputs match for the queries of interest, while the actual method fits a finite, context-dependent query sample. There is no bound or systematic out-of-distribution evaluation for future queries, repeated compactions, or domain shifts. The AIME online-compaction result is encouraging but only a small proof of concept.

The stated NNLS subproblem is not always actually solved: for OMP the implementation uses an unconstrained least-squares solution followed by clipping with zero projected-gradient iterations. This is not generally the NNLS optimum described in the method and weakens the precision of the algorithmic account, though the empirical procedure can still work.

Reproducibility is only moderate. Many implementation details are documented, but there is no clear code-release statement, the actual learned head-budget schedules are not supplied numerically, the calibration/evaluation separation for those schedules is unclear, and decoding seeds and exact stochastic evaluation settings are missing.

The ethics discussion is thin for possible clinical or agent-memory applications. LongHealth is used only as a benchmark, so this is not a material ethical blocker, but the paper should explicitly caution that lossy compaction can omit clinically or operationally critical details and should discuss privacy and retention implications of latent caches.

strengths: Soundness: The central formulation is well motivated. Decomposing concatenated attention into locally normalized output and attention mass justifies matching both quantities, and the per-token bias directly addresses the mass deficit caused by retaining fewer keys.

Originality: Attention-mass preservation combined with closed-form value fitting, nonnegative bias fitting, and OMP-based key selection is a novel and coherent alternative to end-to-end latent-cache optimization.

Significance: The method addresses an important deployment bottleneck and establishes a strong quality–compaction-time trade-off, including useful results at 20–100× compaction and a promising repeated-compaction AIME demonstration.

Evaluation breadth is strong: results cover three model families and QuALITY, LongHealth, QASPER, LongBench v2, RULER, and AIME, with comparisons to summarization, Cartridges, eviction methods, and token merging. Component, query-sampling, aggregation, and nonuniform-budget ablations generally support the design choices.

Presentation and reproducibility are mostly strong: the manuscript is clear and polished, provides algorithms, prompts, numerical settings, dataset protocols, timing breakdowns, and implementation details. It also candidly discusses slower variants, degradation at extreme compression, architectural incompatibility with MLA, and remaining systems-integration work.
weaknesses: Several headline comparisons lack uncertainty estimates. QuALITY uses only 50 contexts, LongHealth only four aggregated contexts, and Cartridges is evaluated on a higher-performing 20-context QuALITY subset and only one model. This weakens claims of uniformly outperforming Cartridges and makes some small accuracy differences difficult to interpret.

The LongBench v2 analysis selects 47 examples using full-context versus no-context outcomes and then evaluates with stochastic decoding. Although all methods are rerun on that subset, the selection creates a conditional benchmark with limited statistical power and unclear generalization to the full task distribution.

The practical serving claims are not fully demonstrated. Timings measure offline compaction kernels, but the paper does not report end-to-end decoding throughput, memory, transfer overhead, or latency in an inference engine supporting per-token biases and packed nonuniform per-head cache lengths.

The guarantee for arbitrary appended tokens is conditional on accurately matching the relevant future-query distribution. Reference queries are heuristic, and the paper provides no approximation bound or broad out-of-distribution query stress test; thus the theoretical identity does not itself establish robust future behavior.

There are reproducibility inconsistencies: Algorithm 2 loops for t iterations while selecting k keys each iteration, apparently producing kt rather than t keys, and the stated NNLS routine with zero iterations is actually unconstrained least squares followed by clamping rather than an exact NNLS solution. No code-release statement is provided.

Ethical and failure-mode treatment is thin for deployment-sensitive settings. Compaction can silently omit specific information, yet instruction-following evidence is qualitative and there is no targeted safety analysis, especially relevant given the clinical-document evaluation.
